paragraphs: _(e) The Russian Monk and his possible Significance_

Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In the educated world these days, some people say the word with a sneer and others use it as a curse, and this contempt for monks keeps growing. It is true, sadly true, that many monks are sluggards, gluttons, libertines and insolent beggars. Educated people point at these and say: “You are idlers, useless to society. You live off other people’s labor. You are shameless beggars.” Yet there are so many gentle, humble monks who long for solitude and for fervent prayer in peace! People notice them less, or say nothing about them. And how surprised people would be if I told them that the salvation of Russia may come once more from these gentle monks who long to pray alone! For in peace and quiet they are truly being made ready “for the day and the hour, the month and the year.” In the meantime, in their solitude, they keep the image of Christ fair and undefiled, in the purity of God’s truth, just as it came down to them from the Fathers of old, the Apostles and the martyrs. When the time comes, they will show it to the tottering creeds of the world. That is a great thought. That star will rise out of the East.

That is how I see the monk. Is my view false? Is it too proud? Look at the worldly, at everyone who sets himself above the people of God. Has God’s image, and His truth, not been distorted in them? They have science, but science holds nothing except what the senses can grasp. The spiritual world, the higher part of man’s being, they reject entirely. They dismiss it with a kind of triumph, even with hatred. The world has proclaimed the reign of freedom, especially in recent times. But what do we see in this freedom of theirs? Nothing but slavery and self-destruction! For this is what the world says:

“You have desires, so satisfy them, for you have the same rights as the richest and most powerful. Do not be afraid to satisfy them. Multiply your desires, even.” That is the world’s modern doctrine, and in it they see freedom. And what comes of this right to multiply desires? Among the rich, isolation and spiritual suicide. Among the poor, envy and murder. For the poor have been handed rights, but nobody has shown them how to satisfy their wants. The world’s people insist that it is growing more and more united, more and more tied together in brotherly community, now that it has overcome distance and can send thoughts flying through the air.

Alas, put no faith in a union of that kind. Men understand freedom as the multiplying and quick satisfying of desires, and so they warp their own nature. They breed in themselves many senseless, foolish desires and habits and absurd fancies. They live only for mutual envy, for luxury and show. Having dinners, visits, carriages, rank and slaves to wait on you is thought a necessity. For it they sacrifice life, honor and human feeling, and some even kill themselves when they cannot have it. We see the same among those who are not rich, while the poor drown their unsatisfied need and their envy in drink. But soon they will drink blood in place of wine. They are being led toward it. I ask you, is such a man free? I knew a “champion of freedom” who told me himself that when he was denied tobacco in prison, he suffered so badly from the lack of it that he nearly betrayed his cause to get tobacco again! Yet a man like that says, “I am fighting for the cause of humanity.”

How can such a man fight? What use is he? He may be good for some action that is quickly over, but he cannot last. It is no wonder that instead of winning freedom they have sunk into slavery. Instead of serving brotherly love and the union of mankind, they have fallen, on the contrary, into quarrels and isolation. My mysterious visitor and teacher told me so when I was young. And so the idea of serving humanity, of brotherly love and the solidarity of mankind, is fading more and more from the world. Sometimes it is even met with derision. For how can a man shake off his habits? What can become of him when he is so enslaved to satisfying the countless desires he has made for himself? He is isolated. What does the rest of humanity matter to him? They have managed to pile up a bigger heap of things, but there is less joy in the world.

The monastic way is very different. People laugh at obedience, fasting and prayer, yet only through them lies the road to real, true freedom. I cut away my superfluous, unnecessary desires. I subdue my proud and wanton will and chastise it with obedience. With God’s help I reach freedom of spirit, and with it spiritual joy. Who is better able to conceive a great idea and serve it, the rich man in his isolation, or the man who has freed himself from the tyranny of material things and habits? People reproach the monk for his solitude: “You have shut yourself away behind monastery walls to save your own soul, and forgotten the brotherly service of humanity!” But we shall see who proves the more zealous for brotherly love. For it is not we who are isolated but they, though they cannot see it. In the old days the leaders of the people came from among us, and why not again? The same gentle, humble ascetics will rise up and go out to work for the great cause. The salvation of Russia comes from the people, and the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We are isolated only if the people are isolated. The people believe as we do. A reformer who does not believe will never accomplish anything in Russia, however sincere his heart and however great his genius. Remember that! The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will be one and Orthodox. Take care of the peasant and guard his heart. Go on educating him quietly. That is your duty as monks, for the peasant has God in his heart.
(_f_) _Of Masters and Servants, and of whether it is possible for them to be Brothers in the Spirit_

Of course I do not deny that the peasants have their sin too. The fire of corruption is spreading before our eyes, hour by hour, working its way down from above. The spirit of isolation is coming upon the people as well. Moneylenders and devourers of the commune are rising up. The merchant is already hungrier and hungrier for rank. He tries to look cultured without a trace of culture in him, and to that end he meanly despises his old traditions and is even ashamed of the faith of his fathers. He calls on princes, though he is only a peasant gone bad. The peasants are rotting in drunkenness and cannot break the habit. And the cruelty to their wives, even to their children! All from drunkenness! In the factories I have seen children of nine, frail, rickety, stooped and already depraved. The stuffy workshop, the din of the machines, work all day long, the foul language and the drink, the drink. Is that what a little child’s heart needs? He needs sunshine, children’s games, good examples all around him, and at least a little love. This must stop, monks. No more torturing of children. Rise up and preach against it. Hurry, hurry!

But God will save Russia. The peasants are corrupted and cannot give up their filthy sin, yet they know that God curses it and that they do wrong when they sin. So our people still believe in righteousness, still have faith in God and still weep tears of devotion.

The upper classes are another matter. They follow science and want to build justice on reason alone, without Christ as before, and they have already proclaimed that there is no crime and no sin. That is consistent, for if you have no God, what does crime mean? In Europe the people are already rising against the rich with violence, and their leaders everywhere are leading them to bloodshed and teaching them that their wrath is righteous. But their “wrath is accursed, for it is cruel.” God will save Russia, as He has saved her many times. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and their meekness.

Fathers and teachers, watch over the people’s faith, and this will not be a dream. All my life our great people have struck me with their dignity, a true and seemly dignity. I have seen it myself, I can bear witness to it, I have seen it and marveled at it, I have seen it in spite of the degrading sins and the poverty-stricken look of our peasants. They are not servile. Even after two centuries of serfdom they are free in manner and bearing, without insolence, and neither revengeful nor envious. “You are rich and noble, you are clever and talented. Well, be so, God bless you. I respect you, but I know that I too am a man. By respecting you without envy, I prove my dignity as a man.”

In truth, if they do not say this (they do not yet know how to say it), they act it. I have seen it myself and known it myself. And, would you believe it, the poorer the Russian peasant is, the plainer this serene goodness shows. The rich among them are mostly corrupted already, and much of that comes from our own carelessness and indifference. But God will save His people, for Russia is great in her humility. I dream of seeing our future, and I seem already to see it clearly. It will come to pass that even the most corrupt of our rich men will end up ashamed of his riches before the poor. The poor, seeing his humility, will understand and give way to him, and will answer his honorable shame with joy and kindness. Believe me, it will end like that. Things are moving that way. Equality is found only in the spiritual dignity of man, and only among us will that be understood. If we were brothers, there would be fraternity. Before that, they will never agree on dividing wealth. We keep the image of Christ, and it will shine out to the whole world like a precious diamond. So may it be, so may it be!

Fathers and teachers, something touching once happened to me. On my wanderings I met my old orderly, Afanasy, in the town of K. Eight years had passed since I parted from him. He happened to see me in the marketplace, knew me, ran up to me, and how delighted he was! He simply pounced on me: “Master dear, is it you? Is it really you I see?” He took me home with him.

He was out of the army now. He was married and already had two little children. He and his wife made their living as peddlers in the marketplace. His room was poor, but bright and clean. He sat me down, put on the samovar and sent for his wife, as if my visit were a feast day for them. He brought me his children: “Bless them, Father.”

“Is it for me to bless them? I am only a humble monk. I will pray for them. And for you, Afanasy Pavlovitch, I have prayed every day since that day, for it all came from you,” I said. And I explained that to him as well as I could. And what do you think? The man kept staring at me and could not believe that I, his former master and an officer, stood before him in such clothes and such a position. It made him weep.
“Why are you crying?” I said. “Be glad for me instead, dear friend, whom I can never forget, for my path is a glad and joyful one.”
He did not say much. He just kept sighing and shaking his head over me, tenderly.
“What happened to your fortune?” he asked.
“I gave it to the monastery,” I answered. “We live in common.”

After tea I began to say good-by. Suddenly he brought out half a rouble as a gift for the monastery, and I saw him hurriedly press another half-rouble into my hand: “That is for you on your wanderings. It may come in useful, Father.”

I took his half-rouble, bowed to him and his wife, and went out rejoicing. As I walked I thought: “Here we both are, he at home and I on the road, sighing and shaking our heads, no doubt, and yet smiling in the joy of our hearts as we remember how God brought us together.”

I have never seen him again since. I had been his master and he my servant, but when we exchanged a loving kiss with softened hearts, a great human bond was between us. I have thought about this a great deal, and this is what I think now: is it so unthinkable that this grand, simple-hearted unity might in time become universal among the Russian people? I believe that it will come to pass, and that the time is near.

About servants I will add this. In the old days, when I was young, I often lost my temper with servants: “the cook had served something too hot, the orderly had not brushed my clothes.” What taught me better then was a thought of my dear brother’s, which I had heard from him in childhood: “Am I worth it, that another should serve me and be ordered about by me in his poverty and ignorance?” And I wondered at the time that such simple, self-evident ideas are so slow to come to our minds.

There cannot fail to be servants in the world, but act so that your servant is freer in spirit than he would be if he were no servant. Why can I not be a servant to my servant and even let him see it, with no pride on my side and no mistrust on his? Why should my servant not be like my own kin, so that I take him into my family and am glad to do so? This can be done even now, and it will lead to the grand unity of men in the future. Then a man will not look for servants for himself, nor wish to turn his fellow creatures into servants as he does now. He will long, on the contrary, with his whole heart, to be the servant of all, as the Gospel teaches.

And can it be a dream that in the end man will find his joy only in deeds of light and mercy, and not, as now, in cruel pleasures: in gluttony, fornication, ostentation, boasting and the envious rivalry of one man with another? I firmly believe it is not a dream, and that the time is near. People laugh and ask: “When will that time come? Does it look like coming?” I believe that with Christ’s help we shall achieve this great thing. And think how many ideas in the history of mankind were unthinkable ten years before they appeared! Yet when their appointed hour came, they came forth and spread over the whole earth. So it will be with us. Our people will shine out in the world, and all men will say: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the corner-stone of the building.”

And we may put a question to the scornful themselves: if our hope is a dream, when will you build your edifice and order things justly by your intellect alone, without Christ? If they declare that they are the ones advancing toward unity, only the simplest-hearted among them believe it. One can truly marvel at such simplicity. In truth, their dreams are more fantastic than ours. They aim at justice, but they deny Christ, and they will end by flooding the earth with blood, for blood cries out for blood, and he that taketh up the sword shall perish by the sword. Without Christ’s covenant they would slaughter one another down to the last two men on earth. Those last two men would not be able to restrain each other in their pride, and one would kill the other and then himself. That would come to pass, were it not for Christ’s promise that for the sake of the humble and meek the days shall be shortened.

When I was still in an officer’s uniform, soon after my duel, I spoke about servants in company, and I remember that everyone was amazed at me. “What!” they asked. “Are we to sit our servants down on the sofa and offer them tea?” And I answered: “Why not, sometimes at least?” Everyone laughed. Their question was frivolous and my answer was not clear, but the thought in it was to some extent right.
(_g_) _Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds_

Young man, never forget prayer. Whenever you pray sincerely, there will be new feeling and new meaning in it, which will give you fresh courage, and you will understand that prayer is an education. Remember also, every day and whenever you can, to say to yourself, “Lord, have mercy on all who appear before You today.” For every hour and every moment, thousands of men leave life on this earth, and their souls appear before God. And how many of them go in solitude, unknown, sad and dejected, because no one grieves for them or even knows whether they ever lived! And behold, from the other end of the earth perhaps, your prayer for their rest will rise to God, though you did not know them and they did not know you. How touching it must be for a soul that stands in dread before the Lord to feel, at that moment, that someone is praying for him too, that a fellow creature is left on earth who loves him too! And God will look more graciously on you both. For if you have felt so much pity for him, how much more pity will He feel, Who is infinitely more loving and merciful than you! And He will forgive him for your sake.
